newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen voters choose from snakes, swords, rockets.
newsitem.headline: Yemen voters choose from snakes, swords, rockets.

text.p: Snakes, swords and rockets are being used to help illiterate voters identify candidates in Yemen's first general election since a 1994 civil war nearly tore the country apart.

Most of the 3,473 candidates, 17 of them women, are relying on scores of easy-to-identify symbols for the first time in the poor Arab state's modern history to ensure free and fair elections on Sunday.

But they are steering clear of using dogs, donkeys and monkeys because of negative connotations on the tens of thousands of posters, banners and election programmes that have transformed the campaign into a colourful fiesta.

Appealing to Yemenis on television and radio and in rallies since campaigning began last week, most candidates are pledging to improve the quality of life by fighting inflation and unemployment and protecting national unity.
"By using election symbols, we are protecting the freedom of choice in the ballot as many of the voters are illiterate," said parliament deputy Mohammad Qahtan.

"This will allow illiterate voters at ballot boxes to circle the symbol on the voting cards without having to rely on anyone to do it for them," added Qahtan, who last year voted in favour of amendments to the law allowing the use of symbols.

Some 4.6 million of the 7.5 million people aged 18 and over who are eligible to vote out of Yemen's 16 million population had registered for the poll when the process ended last August. But only 2.62 million people got their voting cards, officials said.
Candidates are campaigning for 301 parliamentary seats under the banners of 12 parties or as independents.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party (YSP), some of whose former leaders launched the southern separatist campaign that sparked the civil war, and four others have announced they will boycott the poll because of alleged irregularities.
But party officials said 20 YSP members are running as independents, raising concern among the group's leadership.
The ruling General People's Congress (GPC) of President Ali Abdullah Saleh has chosen the horse as its election symbol and its junior coalition partner the Islamist Islah party is using the sun.

One independent is using a mobile phone, still a novelty in Yemen, as his election symbol while another is using the Janbiyyah, a curved dagger worn by Yemeni men at their waist as part of their national dress.

Most symbols reflect Yemen's varied socio-economic and political culture and its diverse wildlife or address popular day-to-day worries such as the price of bread and vegetables in one of the Arab world's poorest countries.
Symbols include horses, camels, lions, falcons, fish, birds, palm trees, flowers, candles, sticks, knives, boats, dinosaurs, pistols, rifles, chalk and water wells.

Despite difficulties that could arise when the new symbol system is tested, most officials and candidates agree it will drastically cut down on possible voter manipulation -- a frequent complaint in past polls.

"It will ensure fairer elections without any manipulation of voters, especially illiterates who carry a heavy weight in (determining results)," said Said al-Hakimi, who is in charge of supervising the ballot.
"This will also help us tackle many of the negative aspects witnessed in previous elections," he told Reuters.
Many parties and politicians claimed illiterate voters were abused in the 1993 elections in favour of certain candidates.
According to official figures, 836,000 of the 2.27 million people who took part in that poll were illiterate. Most hailed from rural areas although illiteracy also remains high in main cities.
Western diplomats expect the GPC to return as the governing party and then move further to meet World Bank demands for economic reforms, a sensitive subject in Yemen.
Saleh has invited international observers to Yemen to ensure a fair ballot. International observers monitored the last poll in 1993 when 22 parties competed for 301 seats in parliament.
